title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The failure here is one of training-data sourcing: an AI music generation system was built using copyrighted recordings scraped from the internet, including from platforms such as YouTube, Deezer, and Genius, without the permission of rights holders. The result is a deployed product that can reproduce sections of specific well-known recordings closely enough that plaintiffs were able to demonstrate near-identical outputs by supplying only descriptive prompts about genre, decade, and artist style. This is a case of a system being deployed outside the conditions its source material was licensed for, at the point where training data was assembled.

The failure would have required intervention before training began, specifically a decision about whether to license the source material or exclude protected works. No technical guardrail applied after training can undo the reproduction of copyrighted content that has already been encoded into model weights. The outputs demonstrate that the boundary between learning musical patterns and memorizing specific recordings was crossed, at least in some cases, though the precise mechanism is contested.

What is not established is intent: the lawsuits allege willful infringement, but allegations are not findings, and no final verdict on that question has been reached in the US proceedings. A German court ruled against Suno on copyright grounds in one case, and one major label reached a settlement with Suno that included a joint venture, but the broader US litigation and class actions from independent artists remain unresolved.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Warner Music, and Sony Music have filed lawsuits against two popular AI music generators, Udio and Suno, claiming they illegally scraped thousands of copyrighted songs to train their systems. The labels allege the companies deliberately copied massive amounts of music without permission or compensation, and that the AI models directly reproduce sections of famous songs. The labels submitted a comprehensive list of thousands of copyrighted works they claim were used, featuring artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Michael Jackson, and Coldplay.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate famous songs by using specific prompts describing musical characteristics like decade, genre, and artist style. They generated examples including near-identical versions of Green Day's "American Idiot" and Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits, filed in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, represent a major legal battle over how generative AI services use copyrighted material. Both companies previously claimed their training constituted fair use, but the record labels argue this amounts to willful copyright infringement on an unprecedented scale.
